en: The Sūtra on the Four Self-Inflicted Injuries, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. The Buddha said:
"To not study day or night, to not cease from lust in old age, to not give away wealth when one has it, and to not receive the Buddha..."
It is said that these four ways of departing from the mind result in returning to harm oneself.

In ancient times, those who were wealthy and noble were arrogant, haughty, and self-indulgent; kings, sovereigns, and worldly fools knew only how quickly day and night passed, yet they failed to realize their lives were ending. They were constantly prone to anger, stubborn and self-opinionated, lustful, conceited, and greedy for wealth—where are they now?
Disliking the Way of the Sūtras and loathing to hear of self-restraint, their minds wander at will and they are heedless without inhibition;
at such times, they are unaware of hunger and thirst, nor can they reflect upon the sores and wounds of the nine orifices and their foul, impure nature.

Whether walking, standing, lying down, or awake, they engage in hundreds of various matters that plant the roots of suffering and affliction; they are arrogant toward the Great Dharma and do not understand how to cherish their own bodies.

When old age and sickness arrive, one's physical appearance changes; the desires for the five pleasures cannot be obtained forever. When illness strikes and one is confined to bed, there is agitation and no peace. When the decree of death suddenly arrives, the body must perish; how could it endure for long?
Birth and death continue without end, and the evil realms do not cease; one's own lifespan, as well as birth and death, suffering, affliction, and distress—all these depend entirely upon oneself.
"Observing it from this perspective, what constitutes a person?
Sensual pleasures, amusements, songs, dances, and performances—how long do they last?
They are like a single breath."

Through the clarity of wisdom, she changed her aspirations and resolved to maintain her own integrity and purity; she realized that all things in this world ultimately return to emptiness and nothingness.
Even if there were songs and performances, people would find no joy in them and take no pleasure in them, and the singers themselves would feel ashamed.
The multitude are deluded, constantly delighting in music and entertainment; only when illness and sorrow arrive do they feel grief and distress.

During times of peace and security, they engage in myriad affairs and fail to provide for their own welfare; having already invited ten thousand offenses, calamities and misfortunes respond like echoes, yet they cannot discern the causes that have brought these upon themselves.
The body is like a painted vase, filled within with impurities, a foul place of pus and blood, resembling a leather bag wrapped around filth.

One does not realize that this body, both inside and out, must eventually perish; yet one constantly adorns it with pigments and cosmetics, considering oneself handsome and peerless in countenance, failing to observe the diseases and discharges flowing from the nine orifices.
"Those of such a kind are entangled in a net and are unable to contemplate their own bodies.
They are like magical illusions, flickering and non-apparent; only the Daoist, observing that worldly people are thus deluded, constantly reflects upon his own body."

Observe closely how all these bustling and chaotic beings contend only over trivial matters that do not even concern their throats; yet disaster issues from the mouth, and a thousand calamities and myriad sins return to entangle them once more.
Whether they harm one another or become enemies out of anger, all such things arise from greed and compete for profit and desire.
The deluded masses follow suit, failing to recognize the truth of the Way and its principles or the confusion of worldly falsehoods; thus, old age and death suddenly arrive, and they find no freedom.

The benevolent, the worthy, and the wise, if they can clearly understand that wealth and possessions are impermanent—sudden like a storm of wind and rain, like lightning, like a dream, like a magical illusion, or like a mirage—[will not be attached].

When impermanence arrives, it is something no one welcomes; from beginning to end, they are linked in a chain, bound and fettered as they follow one another, never escaping the prison of the five aggregates and the six sense-decays.

"Disrespectful toward one's teacher, they distance themselves from the wisdom of the Way; craving their own physical form and flesh, they do not cease their lewd behavior. Their six faculties—ear, eye, nose, mouth, body, and mind—plant nothing but calamities and afflictions, more numerous than the seeds of all the trees and grasses in the world.
Their hearts of affection and attachment are both vast and long-lasting, comparable to the rivers and seas."

From birth until old age, one encounters myriad circumstances; though one may possess a countenance that is upright and beautiful, one should with composure observe its impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and lack of self.

Yet they are instead deluded, perceiving only perverse benefits for themselves; they drown in the five musical tones, conceal their capacities within, and fail to restrain the mind. Wandering aimlessly in all directions, they employ worldly expedients; they do not dwell upon the mindfulness of time and moment, nor do they abide in the auspiciousness of every step.

"I vow to humble my mind and exert all my strength to eliminate the afflictions of various calamities; nothing is more like this than an infant who cannot distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly, or the impurity of excrement and urine!
By diligently practicing with vigor and abandoning evil so that it has no place to remain, one may be freed from the afflictions of distress, birth, old age, sickness, death, decay, and ruin."
Reflecting upon this myself, [I see that] from the Heaven of the Thirty-three up to the Heaven of No-Thought, all are subject to the difficulties of beginning and ending within these three realms.
One must resolve to study the Way; yet if one’s recognition of the Way is not thorough, and if one is greedy for the body and distracted in mind, one will fall back into the six sense-faculties.
One should contemplate with clarity and rectify the mind regarding birth and death; then there will be no further coming and going, and the cycle of beginning and ending shall be severed.
People are attached to sensory flavors and their various passions remain unceasing; conversely, they fear the prohibitions and precepts.
Their manifold doubts are not eliminated, and they breathelessly calculate things as permanent, observing only the affairs before their eyes.
For this reason, as long as one does not cease the five realms of existence, one will repeatedly obtain a body.
By pruning the six sense-faculties, uprooting the five aggregates, and practicing cultivation, one attains peace.

Upon seeing that which is desirable, one should examine oneself; by not receiving the six sense bases, there will be no sorrow or fear. Being without fear, one enters the site of enlightenment and attains the gateway to wisdom.
The student hesitates, their mind lacking constancy and focus, sometimes advancing and sometimes retreating; thus they become deluded, coming and going without end. To speak by way of analogy:

it is like having once been an enemy, yet later reconciling until one becomes deeply intimate; or like being a man before, yet later becoming terrified and timid. To direct the mind toward the Way, only to deviate from it midway and fall back into the six sense bases—this is what is meant.

They fall back into the afflictions of birth and death within the five realms, drinking bitterness and consuming poison, mutually devouring one another, showing no regard for kinsmen and making no distinction between their own clans, remaining entirely unaware of themselves.

The towering and holy Buddha beheld this with his own eyes; grieving that sentient beings had lost the Way, he bestowed the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—to take pity upon the myriad people.
Regarding the omens of the sprouting stage, before the various classes of beings have appeared, if one harbors even a single portion of resolve that does not waver:

"Suppose there is someone who, with a sincere heart, desires to cross over [to liberation]; they should contemplate and deliberate deeply, practicing the Way with a single mind. They must not speak of their family, kinsmen, or the bonds of affection; rather, they should know that all is impermanent. This borrowed body is but a temporary gathering of conditions, destined for separation."
Suffering and affliction persist; beings exist in mutual dependence, and all things return to emptiness—none of them are "mine.
One who clearly understands this non-existence shall deliver the people of the ten directions throughout the world.

Those who practice the paths of karma do not doubt the act of giving, harbor no anger, and abandon the heart of greedy attachment; thus they sever all causal conditions. The practitioner of the Way observes what is appropriate and what is not, examining himself within.
It is like a dream or an illusion; it is like a military expedition where a host of a million men relies upon a renowned general to repel the enemy.

So too does the practitioner subdue the mind and restrain the will, cultivating the Dharma and honoring the Way, practicing the precepts in accordance with them. With body and mind pure and bright, he bestows kindness and virtue, casting aside anger, arrogance, and contention. He applies himself single-mindedly to the practice of the Way without allowing obstacles to arise, his resolve fixed upon the path of discipline.
If one leads a multitude as a general, one must first rectify one's own mind before acting through the body. When both body and mind are upright, there will be no loss.
Having no loss, one has no need for a following; having attained the Way and departed from the mundane, being uniquely valiant and peerless, one then knows that the Way is supreme.

"Just as the practices of worldly people differ—some worshiping celestial deities, earth, water, fire, wind, the sun and moon, mountains and rivers, or various spirits—it is of no benefit whatsoever. Thus they remain within the cycle of birth and death, unable to escape the net or the prison. They merely wish for long life, peace, and self-indulgence, hoping to obtain a lifespan of a hundred thousand years; how insignificant such things are!"
One must inevitably return to death.
Practicing the Way for a single day is superior to living for a hundred years.

Failing to reckon with impermanence, one instead indulges in greed and attachment, claiming to have parents, brothers, wives, children, and kinsmen both near and far. Yet when illness suddenly arrives and one lies weak and exhausted upon the bed, speaking at dawn to one's relatives to ask them to share one's pain, they all say they cannot; only then does the sick person realize the truth.

"There are five kinds of relatives who, while intending to benefit you, constantly sit by you as you labor to earn a living, providing for you sufficiently at all times, yet cause your bodies to fall into greed, thereby binding themselves and harming themselves."

Anxious concern for one's nine clans obstructs and abandons virtuous practice and ruins the resolve for the Way; when old age, sickness, death, and the fruits of good and evil—suffering and pleasure—arrive, one must face them alone, with no one to take their place.
Those who have not yet attained the Way all harbor this thought: they are unable to practice giving or maintain the Way as a virtue.

Those who are able to give will enjoy long-lasting peace and security in both this life and future lives; it serves as provisions for the cycle of birth and death. From generation to generation, they shall be noble and wealthy, acquiring innumerable carriages, elephants, horses, houses, and treasures of gold and silver. Their parents, brothers, wives, children, and friends shall all receive peace and security through their merit.
If there are those who practice giving, even bystanders who rejoice in it obtain immeasurable merit, let alone the donor themselves.

When one personally prepares the offerings with one's own hands, the blessings one receives in future lives will follow that person as a retribution, just as a shadow follows a form or an echo responds to a sound.
That which is without the hindrances of the aggregates (skandha-āvaraṇa) is called Nirvāṇa.

This Nirvāṇa likewise lacks the five aggregates, the sun, moon, and stars, wind, cold, light, and darkness; it is neither empty nor substantial, it has no years, and it eliminates old age, sickness, and death. It is like an echo that cannot be heard; it is no longer a body of aggregates, for it is in union with the Way.
This constitutes long life, constant peace and security, enduring existence for eternity, and immeasurable happiness—things not understood by the mundane.
When a person of wisdom realizes this and explains it through discernment, they may attain the Way of the Buddha, the True Person.
The foolish do not practice the Way, but instead plan only for their own bodies, longing for old age, sickness, and death.

Their harmful karmic deeds and various sufferings are like planting the five grains: one returns to eat what one has sown. Such is the nature of good and evil; each receives their own retribution accordingly.

Since one has already sown the seeds of affliction, one should not fear them; yet, one further fears old age, sickness, and death. This body composed of the four elements cannot escape these calamities.
Water, fire, thieves, enemies, creditors, and government officials—all such myriad things—one likewise fears, yet remains unaware that this is suffering.

This arises from one's own nature, yet one turns back to pursue sensual desires; while living in this world, one creates such causes for sorrow. This is not granted by Heaven, nor is it caused by the Way; it is obtained naturally through what one has practiced since the beginning.

"O noble lady, for one who studies the Way and seeks transcendence of the world, it is extremely easy and not difficult; nor does it require arduous toil. If one constantly applies diligent intent, seeking with vigor, faithfully accepts the holy teaching, and subdues the mind with heroic courage, one shall attain clear wisdom and the reward of precious excellence."
For example, like the majesty of a lion, there are no wild beasts that it does not subdue;
likewise, just as worldly people cannot comprehend that suffering is suffering, they are like pigs in a sty who do not realize that excrement is foul-smelling.

Furthermore, it is like a moth flying into a lamp’s flame; so too do those of ignorant and deluded mind follow their own inclinations, and upon encountering illicit lust, they cast themselves into the prison of craving. Greedy for birth and death, they do not realize they are being tormented by them, yet they claim for themselves that they are free from sorrow, supreme, and unsurpassed.

With empty minds and perverse steps, they gaze far and wide with wide-open eyes, yet they do not know the methods for advancing or retreating, or seeking survival beyond the realm of heaven, earth, sun, and moon. They merely desire to be in constant turmoil, vying with one another to claim superiority and nobility; they covet fame and glory, acting with arrogant pride and self-indulgence, wishing to make all people submit to them, exerting their authority over heaven and earth so that others fear them and hope to serve them with reverence, believing themselves to have reached fulfillment within their own time.

“The Buddha beholds the myriad affairs of the world, all of which are situated in unworthiness; they ought to follow the transformation of the Way, yet instead they habitually practice the defiled and dishonorable conduct discarded by the former sages.”

The people of the world are pitiable; trembling with anxiety, they seek profit, desiring to increase their possessions and greedily craving swift wealth. They become ever more attached to the five desires and wander through the mundane path, finding no means to emerge from it on their own.
Like prisoners in a jail, even if their shackles and wooden stocks were removed, how could they possibly liberate themselves?
How bitter! Beings such as these set their minds upon birth and death, like a chariot wheel that turns without end or limit.
To sever this course of action and cast off all desires is like opening the gates of a prison or a bird escaping from a net.
"Those who study the Way but remain attached to their kin, wives, and children thereby delude themselves and fail to reach Nirvana.

When those gathered there heard this teaching, they all renewed their single-minded devotion to leaving the secular world, applied themselves with diligent effort, prostrated themselves, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Four Self-Inflicted Injuries Spoken by the Buddha.
